_provenance.note: South Dakota SNAP curated supplements. South Dakota has NO existing packages/snap-rules StatePolicy entry and NO oracle-fixture coverage — a genuine blank slate, like this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, and New Hampshire prior builds. This pack is CORPUS-ONLY and does not touch packages/snap-rules or the oracle fixture. South Dakota is built as part of a five-agent parallel batch (RI, MT, DE, SD, ND) built concurrently by separate agents. Drafted almost entirely from a single direct, clean fetch of DSS's own current SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual PDF (dss.sd.gov, no WAF barrier, HTTP 200), extracted with pdftotext -layout, cross-checked against WebSearch corroboration and one secondary legal-research source (Collateral Consequences Resource Center) for South Dakota Codified Law 28-12-3.

supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP consumer page (dss.sd.gov/economicassistance/snap.aspx); DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §4150; eaPortal (eaportal.sd.gov)
supplements.heading: South Dakota calls its program plainly "SNAP" — no distinctive local brand — and its self-service portal is the eaPortal, run by DSS's Division of Economic Assistance
supplements.text: South Dakota DSS's own consumer materials and its SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive South Dakota-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." South Dakota's current self-service application portal is the eaPortal (eaportal.sd.gov), per manual §4150: applicants can submit the entire application electronically or just page one (name, address, and signature) to begin the process, saving the rest for later submission. Applicants can also apply by mail or in person/by phone at a local DSS office (DSS-EA-301 Economic Assistance Application, revised 11/25). South Dakota's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DSS's Division of Economic Assistance through Economic Assistance Benefits Specialists (EABS) — a state-administered program with no county-level SNAP eligibility-policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, and New Hampshire packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA. Minnehaha, Pennington, and (per the manual's own Chapter Thirteen table of contents) Yankton Counties run Employment & Training (E&T) as a MANDATORY work-registration program for certain participants — a county-level program-operations distinction, not a county-level eligibility-policy variation.

supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §7700 (Categorically Eligible Households); §9010 (Maximum Allowable Resources); §11300 (Budgeting Income)
supplements.heading: STRUCTURAL FLAGSHIP FINDING: South Dakota does NOT run Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) — a strict 130% FPG gross / 100% FPG net income test applies to non-categorically-eligible households, and the current resource limits ($4,500 elderly/disabled, $3,000 all other) correct a stale $2,750/$4,250 figure several current secondary sources still repeat
supplements.text: South Dakota DSS's own manual, §11300, states plainly: "the gross income eligibility standard is 130% of the Federal income poverty level. Households which contain an elderly or disabled member must meet the net income eligibility standard; all other households must meet both the gross and net income standards, unless categorically eligible." Categorical eligibility itself, per §7700, is reserved narrowly for households where every member receives (or is authorized to receive) SSI, TANF, or Tribal TANF benefits, or one member receives Child Care Services (CCS) benefits, or the household's TANF/Tribal TANF application was recently diverted or closed — this pack found NO South Dakota provision expanding categorical eligibility to a broader gross-income ceiling (e.g. 200% FPG) the way BBCE states do, and cross-checked this against WebSearch corroboration naming South Dakota as one of a small group of states nationally (sources vary between six and seven named states, but consistently include South Dakota) that has not adopted BBCE. This pack flags this precisely: South Dakota SNAP applicants face a real, binding 130%/100% FPG income test unless they are categorically eligible in the narrow TANF/SSI/CCS sense, not a broad income-ceiling waiver. Resource limits, per §9010, are $4,500 for households with an eligible disabled member or a member age 60 or over, and $3,000 for all other households; categorically eligible households are exempt from any resource test. This pack flags a genuine, worth-disclosing correction here: multiple current secondary/aggregator sources this pack found in the course of research quote South Dakota's resource limits as $2,750 (most households) and $4,250 (elderly/disabled) — these are STALE figures (consistent with an earlier FFY cycle, likely FFY2023) that several sites have not updated. South Dakota DSS's own manual, dated "Updated July 2026" on its cover page and fetched directly with no access barrier, gives the CURRENT $4,500/$3,000 figures, matching the national FFY2026 cycle this roster's other current-cycle states have independently confirmed. If a household is elderly/disabled but that member is disqualified for certain reasons (ineligible alien, no SSN, fleeing felon, parole/probation violator, trafficking conviction, TANF carryover disqualification, work-registration sanction, IPV disqualification, FDPIR IPV carryover disqualification, ineligible student/roomer/live-in attendant, or DCS non-cooperation disqualification), the household's resource limit drops to the standard $3,000 even with that member present in the household.

supplements.citation: South Dakota Codified Law 28-12-3 (statutory opt-out of Pub. L. 104-193 § 115(a)(2), the federal drug-felony ban, cited to 2020 by a secondary legal-research source); South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §3920/§7370 (Convicted Felon Attestation Procedures — 2014 Farm Bill violent/sex-offense list only)
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CONFIRMATION (of a minority-position claim): South Dakota FULLY opted out of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban — DSS's own manual has NO drug-felony disqualification provision at all, and this pack cross-checked that silence against South Dakota's own codified opt-out statute quoted by a secondary legal source
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) (originally enacted as Pub. L. 104-193 § 115(a)(2), part of the 1996 PRWORA welfare-reform law) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 115(d)(1)(A) (codified as 21 U.S.C. § 862a(d)(1)). This pack read South Dakota DSS's ENTIRE SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual's felon-related provisions closely and found only ONE disqualification category tied to felony convictions: §3920/§7370, "Convicted Felon Attestation Procedures," which applies exclusively to the 2014 Farm Bill's violent/sex-offense list (aggravated sexual abuse under 18 U.S.C. § 2241, murder under 18 U.S.C. § 1111, sexual exploitation of children and related offenses under 18 U.S.C. Chapter 110, and federal/state sexual assault offenses as defined by the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 § 40002(a)) for convictions occurring after February 7, 2014, where the individual is not in compliance with the terms of their sentence or parole. This pack found NO separate drug-felony-conviction disqualification provision anywhere in the manual's roughly 17,000 lines of extracted text. This pack treats a full opt-out as a genuine minority position among states nationally worth confirming rather than accepting at face value, and cross-checked the manual's silence against South Dakota's own codified statute: a secondary legal-research source (the Collateral Consequences Resource Center's national SNAP/TANF drug-felony-ban survey) quotes South Dakota Codified Law 28-12-3 directly as reading, "Pursuant to section 115(d)(1)(A) of Public Law 104-193, South Dakota opts out of the provisions of section 115(a)(2) of Public Law 104-193," and dates South Dakota's opt-out to 2020, moving from a prior full federal ban to a full opt-out for both SNAP and TANF. This pack could NOT independently verify SDCL 28-12-3's text directly against South Dakota's own Legislature site (sdlegislature.gov, whose statute pages did not render plain text for this pack's fetch method) or against Justia (which served a Cloudflare JS-challenge wall this pack could not resolve) — this specific statutory-text citation rests on the CCRC secondary source alone, though it is independently corroborated by the DSS manual's own complete silence on any drug-felony provision; see freshness.json. This is distinct from South Dakota's SEPARATE benefit-trafficking disqualification (trading SNAP benefits for a controlled substance, weapons, ammunition, or explosives, or buying/selling benefits in excess of $499 after 9/23/97, which disqualifies a household from categorical eligibility per §7700(C)(3) and carries its own trafficking-conviction penalty), which this pack flags explicitly as a program-integrity rule distinct from a drug-felony-conviction ban, so the two are not conflated.

supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §10110 (Standard Deduction, effective 10/1/2025), §10210 (Medical Deductions), §10300/§10310 (Shelter Deductions), §10400/§10411 (Utility Deductions)
supplements.heading: INTERNAL-INCONSISTENCY FINDING: DSS's own manual Table of Contents lists SUA/LUA/OUA/PUA figures that CONTRADICT the manual's own body text (stated twice, consistently) — this pack treats the body text as authoritative
supplements.text: South Dakota's Standard Deduction (per DSS's manual §10110, effective as of 10/1/2025) is $209 for household sizes 1 through 3, $223 for size 4, $261 for size 5, and $299 for size 6 or more — matching the current national FFY2026 figures this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Kentucky, Louisiana, Alabama, South Carolina, and New Hampshire packs have each independently confirmed. South Dakota runs a FOUR-tier utility-allowance structure split by qualifying-utility TYPE and COUNT: Standard Utility Allowance (SUA, for households responsible for heating/cooling costs, or an elderly/disabled household member with a LIEAP payment over $20 in the current month or preceding 12 months), Limited Utility Allowance (LUA, at least two non-heating/cooling utility expenses), One Utility Allowance (OUA, exactly one non-heating/cooling utility expense, not allowed if that expense is telephone-only), and Phone Utility Allowance (PUA, telephone/cellular service as the household's only utility expense) — this four-tier, count/type-hybrid structure most closely resembles this roster's Nebraska pack's SUA/LUA/OUA/Telephone structure. This pack flags a genuine internal-document inconsistency it caught rather than silently resolved: the manual's own Table of Contents (page 9 of the PDF) lists these figures as SUA $850, LUA $238, OUA $98, and PUA $54 — but the manual's BODY TEXT states, IDENTICALLY, in two separate locations (the general §10400 overview and the detailed §10411 section), SUA $950, LUA $265, OUA $109, and PUA $60. This pack treats the twice-repeated, internally-consistent body-text figures as the manual's authoritative current numbers and reads the Table of Contents entry as a stale summary page DSS updated the body text of but did not revise the front-matter listing for — a specific, disclosed judgment call rather than an assumption, since this pack cannot independently confirm which figure DSS's live eaPortal benefit-calculation system actually uses without a second, non-manual source. South Dakota's Medical Expense Deduction (§10210, for household members age 60+ or disabled) uses a flat-shortcut mechanism: no deduction for expenses under $35/month, a flat $165 standard deduction (before the $35 disregard, described in the manual as a $200 gross figure minus the $35 disregard) for expenses of at least $36 but less than $201, and actual expenses minus the $35 disregard for expenses over $200 — placing South Dakota with this roster's Kentucky, Louisiana, South Carolina, Missouri, Colorado, Alabama, and New Hampshire packs' flat-shortcut camp, distinct from Nebraska's, Connecticut's, Maryland's, and Indiana's actual-expense-only mechanism. South Dakota's Excess Shelter Deduction is capped at $744/month for households without an elderly/disabled member (matching the current national FFY2026 figure this roster's other states have confirmed), with NO cap for households containing an elderly or disabled member (full amount over 50% of net income after other deductions). South Dakota's Homeless Shelter Deduction is a flat $200 for households with verified shelter costs of at least $199.89 but less than $200, with the household's actual shelter cost used instead once shelter costs exceed $200 — a slightly different mechanism than a flat deduction regardless of actual cost.

supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §13221-13227 (ABAWD Non-Work Exemptions), §13222 (Native American Exemption); USDA FNS/FNA ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index (South Dakota's most recent posted entry is FY2025, dated 08/12/2024, no FY2026 entry)
supplements.heading: South Dakota currently has NO active area-wide ABAWD waiver, and its manual explicitly names a statewide Native American ABAWD exemption applying anywhere in South Dakota, not restricted to reservation residency
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. South Dakota DSS's own manual §13221 confirms the current federal ABAWD age scope of 18-64 (exempt starting the month an individual turns 65), consistent with the OBBBA nationwide rollout this roster has documented in other 2025-2026-built packs. This pack flags §13222 explicitly, directly answering the tribal-land research question this build was asked to check: South Dakota's manual states plainly that "individuals who are Native American who live anywhere in the state are exempt from ABAWD time limits" — NOT restricted to individuals residing on a reservation — defining "Indian"/"Indians" per the federal Indian Health Care Improvement Act definition (tribal, band, or organized-group membership regardless of on/near-reservation residency, including first/second-degree descendants of a member), and separately extending the same exemption to California Indians (per 25 U.S.C. § 1679(a)) and "urban Indians" (per 25 U.S.C. § 1603(18)). ACCESS (South Dakota's eligibility system) codes this exemption as "I – Native American living in any county in South Dakota" on the ABWD panel — the code's own wording explicitly generalizes beyond reservation boundaries. This is a federal ABAWD exemption category (not a South Dakota-specific policy invention), but this pack flags South Dakota's manual as unusually explicit and thorough in spelling out its statewide, not reservation-restricted, scope compared to several other states' manuals this roster has reviewed. Other ABAWD exemptions this pack confirmed directly from the manual: residing with a dependent child under 14 (§13224, applying to ALL adults in the household regardless of parentage), pregnancy (§13226), and a work-registration-exempt category (§13223) covering mandatory TANF WORK registrants, Reemployment Assistance applicants/recipients, at-least-half-time students, caretakers of an incapacitated household member, regular drug/alcohol treatment program participants, individuals temporarily exempt for mental/physical reasons, half-time refugee-training-program participants, and VA Disability benefit recipients regardless of disability rating. On area-wide waivers: USDA FNS/FNA's own ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY 2025-2029 index lists South Dakota's only posted waiver-response entry as FY2025 (dated 08/12/2024), with NO FY2026 entry — in contrast to Minnesota, Montana, and North Dakota, which DO show FY2026 entries on the same current index — consistent with WebSearch corroboration that South Dakota currently has no active statewide or area-wide ABAWD waiver.

terms: food distribution program on indian reservations
supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual §§3902, 5026, 6385-6387
supplements.heading: South Dakota's manual explicitly addresses FDPIR/SNAP mutual exclusivity — a household cannot receive both SNAP and FDPIR commodities in the same month, with a documented exception process
supplements.text: This pack was specifically asked to check whether South Dakota's SNAP manual has state-specific notes on Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR) interaction, given the state's significant tribal-land geography (multiple federally recognized reservations). It does: DSS's manual states in two separate sections (§3902 and §5026, worded almost identically) that an individual may NOT receive SNAP and FDPIR commodities in the same month, unless the individual is in a battered women's shelter. If an individual applies for SNAP in a month they already received commodities (or SNAP with another household), the application must be denied for that month for duplicate eligibility; an applicant who did not personally receive SNAP or commodities in the application month but resides with a household that did may claim separate-household status for one month while the situation is resolved by the second month. A household certified for SNAP but receiving $0 in benefits IS eligible to receive FDPIR commodities. Separately, §§6385-6387 establish an FDPIR Intentional Program Violation (IPV) carryover rule: an individual disqualified from FDPIR for an IPV must be disqualified from SNAP for the same time period — this carryover disqualification also appears in the manual's resource-limit exception list (§9010) as one of the conditions that can reduce an elderly/disabled household's resource limit to the standard $3,000. This pack found this treatment to be a genuine, specific, and reasonably thorough state-manual engagement with the FDPIR/SNAP interaction — not a topic South Dakota's manual is silent on — though this pack did not find any DSS text describing outreach, application support, or administrative coordination specific to South Dakota's individual reservations (e.g. Pine Ridge, Rosebud, Standing Rock, Cheyenne River, Crow Creek, Lower Brule, Yankton, Flandreau) beyond the general FDPIR-interaction rules quoted above; a household-level question about a specific reservation's FDPIR administration would need to be directed to that reservation's own FDPIR office, which this pack did not attempt to enumerate.

supplements.citation: South Dakota DSS SNAP Policy and Procedure Manual (no RMP provision found anywhere in the document); WebSearch corroboration — South Dakota SB 149 (2022) failed in the state Senate, 12-23, and was never enacted
supplements.heading: South Dakota does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program — a prior legislative attempt (SB 149, 2022) failed in the state Senate and was never enacted
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. This pack found consistent corroboration that South Dakota does NOT currently operate an RMP: DSS's own manual explicitly excludes "hot foods ready to eat" and "hot foods and hot food products prepared for immediate consumption" from SNAP-eligible purchases in its general eligible-food-items language, with no RMP carve-out anywhere in the roughly 17,000 lines of manual text this pack reviewed. This pack also found and flags a specific, worth-disclosing legislative history: South Dakota Senate Bill 149, introduced in the 2022 legislative session, would have established an RMP targeted at elderly, disabled, and homeless South Dakotans — but WebSearch corroboration shows the bill FAILED in the state Senate by a vote of 12-23 and was never enacted. This pack flags this explicitly because a search for "South Dakota Restaurant Meals Program" surfaces news coverage of the 2022 bill's introduction that, read in isolation or by an out-of-date secondary source, could be mistaken for evidence that South Dakota has or is about to have an RMP — the bill's actual outcome was a Senate floor defeat, not enactment. South Dakota's manual DOES separately allow homeless SNAP households to use benefits to purchase prepared meals specifically from USDA-approved homeless meal providers (§7411(C)) and allows drug/alcohol treatment center and battered-women's-shelter residents to use benefits at USDA-approved facility food service (§7411(A)-(B)) — these are narrow, federally-defined exceptions for specific institutional/shelter populations, not a general Restaurant Meals Program, and this pack flags the distinction explicitly so the two are not conflated. South Dakota's operative answer for a general applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at an ordinary restaurant is a plain no.
